Connect: ashkajligupta@email.com Product Management Case Study Startupş India Technology Fixing the Monsoon Marketplace Collapse: A Product Case Study on Uber & Rapido in India ASH 8 min read · 1 hour ago -- Listen Share How a rain-soaked evening in Gurugram taught me more about two-sided marketplaces than any textbook could. 🌧️ The Monsoon Standstill: A Personal Frustration Turned Product Breakdown It’s 8:47 PM . The sky has opened up like someone forgot to close a valve. I’m standing under a leaking bus shelter, watching auto-wallahs squeeze through the traffic, phone screen fogged with humidity, watching a small circle spin endlessly on my ride-hailing app. No cars. No drivers. A few auto-wallahs are still trying to negotiate fares outside. Just a loading wheel mocking my optimism. Ten minutes pass. Finally, a ride appears. The fare: 4.2x surge . A trip that normally costs ₹120 now reads ₹504 . I book it anyway, because what choice do I have? Twenty-five minutes later, the driver cancels. “Water logging,” he types. “Cannot come.” This isn’t just one bad night. This is a recurring marketplace problem that happens every single monsoon, across every major Indian city, on both Uber and Rapido. And that frustration is exactly what turned into curiosity: why does a marketplace with millions of daily transactions completely break down under 40mm of rainfall? This article is my attempt to answer that — not as a disgruntled user, but as an aspiring Product Manager dissecting a real, high-stakes systems failure. 📊 Dissecting the Marketplace Collapse: The 3-Sided Problem Ride-hailing isn’t a two-sided marketplace during monsoons. It becomes a three-sided crisis — Users, Drivers, and the Platform all pulling in different, conflicting directions. Let’s break it down the way an engineering team would in a post-mortem. 🧍 The User Side: Demand Spikes, Trust Erodes On a normal evening, you have options. Walk. Grab an auto. Hop on a bike. Catch a bus. Book a cab. The moment heavy rain hits, most of those options quietly disappear — and everyone left standing reaches for the same app at the same time. That’s why demand doesn’t just rise during a downpour — it spikes, by an estimated 3x–5x. The platform’s answer to that spike is surge pricing. But users rarely experience it as “dynamic market efficiency.” They experience it as being charged more precisely when they’re most stuck — which feels a lot less like market logic and a lot more like exploitation during vulnerability. Then comes the second hit: the cancellation. A ride gets booked, hope goes up, and minutes later it’s gone — pushing the wait right back to zero, except now with a canceled trip and a dented sense of trust. That “false hope” loop does more damage than the app simply admitting no drivers are available in the first place. Put it together, and the real cost isn’t just a bad night. It’s long-term trust erosion — even in months where revenue per ride actually goes up. 🚗 The Driver Side: Supply Drops, Real Physical Risk Supply drops sharply because drivers know which roads become difficult or dangerous once the water rises. The core reason isn’t laziness — it’s hydro-locking : when water enters the engine’s air intake and causes catastrophic engine damage if the vehicle is driven through deep water. For many drivers, the vehicle is not just a vehicle — it is the asset that generates their income. A single hydro-locked engine can cost a driver ₹30,000–₹50,000+ in repairs — often more than a week’s or month’s earnings. For a driver, every rainy trip becomes a personal calculation: accept a surge fare and risk asset destruction , or reject and lose income with no safety net in between. There is currently no built-in asset protection mechanism from the platform to offset this risk. 🖥️ The Platform Side: The Algorithm Doesn’t Know It’s Raining Dispatch algorithms are optimized for ETA and distance efficiency , not for real-time hazard awareness . Surge pricing is a blunt way to manage demand — it manages demand mathematically but does nothing to solve the actual supply-side risk problem . The platform has no live integration with municipal flooding data , so it can route drivers into waterlogged lanes with the same confidence as a dry Tuesday afternoon.
